implementation_notes: Ruby exposes the POSIX clocks: Process.clock_gettime(:CLOCK_MONOTONIC) 'returns a clock time as determined by POSIX function clock_gettime()' and accepts unit qualifiers (:float_second by default; use :nanosecond when exactness matters, because a Float cannot represent the full clock precision), while Kernel#sleep 'suspends the current thread for the given number of seconds'. What replaces the classic structure: nothing - write the driver with Ruby's loop and those two calls; there is no stdlib game loop. The pattern's real work in Ruby is remembering that Time.now is wall-clock time and that the GVL serialises CPU-bound threads, so a hand-written loop is a single-threaded scheduler that must not block.
code_sketch:
DT = 1.0 / 60
prev = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
lag = 0.0
loop do
  now = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
  lag += now - prev; prev = now            # monotonic clock, not Time.now
  lag = 0.25 if lag > 0.25                 # clamp: no spiral of death
  drain_input
  while lag >= DT
    step(DT); lag -= DT
  end
  render(lag / DT)
  sleep(DT / 2)                            # at-least sleep; re-measured above
end
pitfalls: Time.now follows the wall clock and can jump; only Process.clock_gettime(:CLOCK_MONOTONIC) gives interval-safe readings.
Kernel#sleep is at-least and coarse; a loop that counts its own iterations drifts, so re-read the monotonic clock every turn.
MRI's GVL means a CPU-heavy step blocks every other Ruby thread, and GC pauses add frame spikes; keep per-step allocations low and offload heavy work.
A loop without a sleep or blocking wait spins at full CPU, while a loop that blocks on IO inside step stops the simulation for every client.

variants.name: Gosu::Window callback loop
variants.implementation_notes: Gosu is the Ruby game library that owns the loop: a Gosu::Window 'manages initialization of all of Gosu's core components and provides timing functionality', Window#show 'enters a modal loop where the Window is visible on screen and receives calls to draw, update etc.', update 'is called once every update_interval milliseconds while the window is being shown' (default 16.666666 ms, i.e. 60 Hz) and draw is 'called after every update and whenever the OS wants the window to repaint itself'. What replaces the classic structure: the library's modal loop replaces the driver and the sleep - implement update for simulation and draw for presentation. The documented separation already encodes fixed update, variable rendering: draw may run more or less often than update.
variants.code_sketch:
class Game < Gosu::Window
  def initialize
    super 1280, 720
    self.update_interval = 1000.0 / 60    # fixed step, in milliseconds
    @world = World.new
  end
  def update                              # called once per fixed interval
    @world.step(1.0 / 60)
  end
  def draw                                # after every update / on repaint
    @world.render(self)
  end
end
Game.new.show
pitfalls: update_interval is in milliseconds while most game math is in seconds; the unit mismatch is silent and a step of 16.6 seconds passes type checks.
The modal loop in Window#show owns the thread: blocking work in update/draw freezes input handling and repaints.
draw may be called independently of update (OS repaint), so it must not advance the simulation; keep state changes in update.
